title: Computable reductions and the undecidability of first-order logic
summary: Translate decision problems by total computable maps, then use the finite Robinson axioms to prove that first-order validity and satisfiability are undecidable.
abstract: A method for deciding one problem can sometimes decide another after a simple translation of its inputs. We make this idea precise and show that every computably enumerable set reduces to the halting problem. The same method connects arithmetic theoremhood with a question about pure logic: is a given sentence true in every structure? Putting the finitely many Robinson axioms into the antecedent gives the required translation. Since their consequences cannot be decided, neither can first-order validity in the language of arithmetic. Valid sentences can still be enumerated by searching for proofs; satisfiable sentences cannot even be enumerated.
